Neonatal female Labords chameleons emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a snout-vent length of just 2 centimeters [Lb = 2 centimeters], a diminutive size that underscores the rapid growth trajectory this species must undertake within its compressed annual life cycle. Incubation experiments conducted under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] reveal that the age at hatching averages approximately 122 days [ab = approximately 122 days], a prolonged embryonic period relative to other small-bodied Malagasy chameleons. This extended developmental phase within the egg likely allows for the formation of a relatively advanced hatchling that is immediately capable of active foraging. The initial body mass at emergence is remarkably low, with neonates weighing about 0.4 grams [Wwb = about 0.4 grams], reflecting the limited resources encapsulated within the small, yolky egg. This energetically frugal start is a necessary adaptation for a species that relies on ephemeral seasonal resources in its arid deciduous forest habitat, where every gram of hatchling mass represents a significant maternal investment.

Periods of accelerated somatic growth are critical for this short-lived species, as female juveniles must attain a snout-vent length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] to trigger the onset of gonadal activation and achieve reproductive maturity. This morphological threshold for puberty is reached approximately 60 days after hatching [tp = approximately 60 days after hatching] when the environmental temperature averages 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a remarkably brief juvenile phase for a lizard of this lineage. In contrast, the ultimate body size attained by adult females is a snout-vent length reaching 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters]. The corresponding adult body mass plateaus at approximately 7.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.6 grams] in fully grown, gravid individuals, indicating that a substantial portion of the adult mass is devoted to developing oocytes and fat stores necessary for a single, explosive reproductive event. The pace of this growth from a 2-centimeter hatchling (2 cm) [Lb = 2 cm] to a reproductively mature adult in under two months is extraordinary among vertebrates and necessitates exceptionally high rates of prey assimilation during the wet season.

The lifespan of Furcifer labordi is one of the shortest recorded for any tetrapod, with field and captive studies converging on a maximum longevity of approximately 219 days [am = approximately 219 days] when maintained at a constant developmental temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This compressed existence, spanning less than one calendar year from hatching to post-reproductive senescence, is tightly synchronized with the pronounced wet-dry seasonality of southwestern Madagascar. The first reproduction event, which constitutes the sole breeding opportunity for most individuals, typically occurs within this window as females produce a single, energetically costly clutch. The lifetime reproductive output under these thermal conditions averages 11 offspring per female  at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a number that reflects the limited abdominal cavity volume available for carrying a full complement of eggs. This low fecundity is offset by a high per-offspring investment, as each newly hatched juvenile must be sufficiently robust to survive the intense competition for invertebrate prey during the brief growing season.

Reproductive effort is concentrated into a single, high-investment event per female, with individuals laying one clutch of eggs per year [F_R_i = one clutch of eggs per year] that typically contains between 11 and 15 eggs [N_R_i = contains between 11 and 15 eggs]. This single clutch pattern is an obligatory life-history strategy given the species' extreme annual mortality; a female that delays reproduction or fails to breed in her only adult season will produce zero lifetime offspring. The adult male reaches a larger ultimate snout-vent length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a pattern of reversed sexual size dimorphism that may relate to male-male combat for access to the seasonally clustered receptive females.

Comparisons with other short-lived chameleons of the genus Furcifer highlight the extreme nature of the Labords chameleon's pace of life. While many congeners exhibit annual or biennial life cycles, F. labordi compresses its entire growth, maturation, reproduction, and mortality into an astonishingly tight seasonal window, with the incubation period itself representing a substantial portion of the total lifespan. Laboratory incubations conducted at a stable 26 °C [T = 26 °C] indicate that the embryonic period lasts 122 days [ab = 122 days], a duration that accounts for roughly half of the total lifespan (approximately 219 days) [am = approximately 219 days] at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], leaving only a few months of free-living activity for growth and reproduction. The neonatal body mass of approximately 0.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.4 grams] places this species among the lightest hatchlings for any terrestrial squamate when considered relative to adult female mass, suggesting that maternal provisioning is heavily skewed toward maximizing egg number rather than individual egg size. The remarkable growth trajectory that carries a hatchling from a snout-vent length of just 2 centimeters [Lb = 2 centimeters] to the pubertal threshold of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] in as little as 60 days ranks among the fastest documented for any terrestrial squamate, a physiological feat that demands continuous high-temperature basking and abundant prey availability throughout the brief wet season.
